description: A heap keeps the minimum or maximum element accessible in O(1) with O(log n) insertion and removal, making it the right structure whenever an algorithm repeatedly needs 'the best remaining item' rather than a fully sorted order. It underpins top-K selection, streaming medians, k-way merges, greedy scheduling, and the priority frontier in Dijkstra-style searches.
important_details: Java's PriorityQueue is a MIN-heap by default; pass Collections.reverseOrder() or a custom Comparator for max-heap behaviour.
Bounding the heap at size k gives O(n log k) time and O(k) space — strictly better than sorting when k is much smaller than n.
Counter-intuitive but essential: for the k LARGEST elements you keep a MIN-heap (so the weakest candidate is at the top, ready to evict), and vice versa.
Heapify (building a heap from an existing array) is O(n), not O(n log n) — worth stating when asked about construction cost.
PriorityQueue.remove(Object) is O(n) in Java; when you need arbitrary deletion, use lazy deletion or a TreeMap instead.
other_relevant_details: Trigger phrases: 'kth largest/smallest', 'top k', 'median of a stream', 'merge k sorted', 'schedule tasks', 'minimum cost to combine'. When the data is static and you only need one query, quickselect (O(n) expected) beats a heap; when data arrives as a stream or you need repeated queries, the heap wins. Always state which of these applies.

variations.description: Maintain a heap of exactly size k while scanning the input, evicting the least relevant element whenever the heap overflows, so that the k best remain at the end.
important_details: k largest -> min-heap of size k; k smallest or k closest -> max-heap of size k.
Offer first, then poll if size exceeds k — this ordering is simpler and less error-prone than checking before inserting.
O(n log k) beats full sorting's O(n log n) whenever k is meaningfully smaller than n, and uses only O(k) space.
Quickselect gives O(n) expected time for a single static query, but cannot handle streaming input — name this trade-off explicitly.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n log k). Space: O(k).

variations.variation: Top K by Frequency (Heap over a Frequency Map)
variations.description: Count occurrences first, then run a bounded heap over the map's entries comparing by count, to extract the k most or least frequent items.
important_details: Two phases: O(n) counting pass, then O(m log k) heap pass over m distinct keys.
Ties often need a secondary comparator (lexicographic order for words) — write the Comparator carefully, since reversing one key but not the other is a frequent bug.
Bucket sort is the O(n) alternative: index buckets by frequency (0..n) and read them from the top down, beating the heap asymptotically.
Mention bucket sort as the optimal follow-up whenever an interviewer asks to improve on O(n log k).
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n + m log k). Space: O(m). Bucket sort achieves O(n) time.

problems.name: Least Number of Unique Integers after K Removals

variations.description: Split the data into a max-heap holding the smaller half and a min-heap holding the larger half, keeping them balanced so the median is always readable from their tops in O(1).
important_details: Invariant 1 (ordering): every element in the low max-heap is <= every element in the high min-heap.
Invariant 2 (balance): the two sizes differ by at most one.

The clean insertion idiom is push-then-transfer: add to the low heap, move its top to the high heap, then move back if the high heap grew too large. This enforces both invariants without branching on values.
For a sliding-window median you additionally need removal, which PriorityQueue does in O(n) — use lazy deletion or two TreeMaps instead.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(log n) per insertion, O(1) per median query. Space: O(n).

variations.description: Merge k sorted sequences into one by seeding a min-heap with the current head of each sequence, then repeatedly extracting the global minimum and refilling from the source it came from.
important_details: Heap entries must carry enough context (value, source index, position within source) to know where to pull the replacement from.
Reduces naive pairwise merging from O(N*k) to O(N log k), where N is the total element count.
Skip empty or null sources when seeding, or the first poll throws.
'Smallest range covering elements from k lists' is the same machinery plus tracking the running maximum of the heap's contents.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(N log k). Space: O(k).

variations.description: Simulate a schedule where at each step you greedily take the currently best task or resource from a heap — the standard shape for CPU cooldown scheduling, string reorganization, and machine assignment.
important_details: A max-heap of remaining counts lets you always dispatch the most frequent item, which is the greedy choice that avoids getting stuck at the end.
A cooldown queue holding (count, readyTime) pairs feeds items back into the heap once their wait expires.
Reorganize String is the same idea: always take the two most frequent distinct characters so no two identical characters land adjacent.
Feasibility check: reorganization is impossible when the most frequent character's count exceeds (n+1)/2 — test this before simulating.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n log k) where k is the number of distinct items. Space: O(k).

problems.name: Minimum Cost to Hire K Workers

variations.variation: Interval Scheduling with a Min-Heap of End Times
variations.description: Sort intervals by start time and push their end times into a min-heap; the heap's size at any moment equals the number of simultaneously active intervals, giving room counts and resource allocation directly.
important_details: Sort by START time first — processing intervals out of order breaks the invariant entirely.
Before adding a new interval, poll every heap top that has already ended (end <= current start), freeing those resources.
The maximum heap size observed across the scan is the answer for 'minimum meeting rooms'.
The alternative sweep-line approach (sort all start/end events, +1/-1 counter) is O(n log n) too and is worth knowing as a second solution.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n log n) dominated by the sort. Space: O(n).

variations.description: Use a min-heap as the exploration frontier so the cheapest unprocessed state is always expanded next — the structural core of Dijkstra, A*, and many grid-cost problems.
important_details: Push (cost, state) pairs; pop the minimum cost state and skip it if you have already finalized it with a lower cost.
Lazy deletion is standard: instead of updating an existing heap entry, push a new one and ignore stale pops via a visited check or a distance comparison.
For 0/1 edge weights, a deque-based 0-1 BFS replaces the heap and drops the log factor.
When the state includes extra dimensions (fuel left, obstacles removed), the visited structure must be keyed on the full state, not just the node.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(E log V), or O(n^2 log n) on an n x n grid. Space: O(V).

variations.description: When elements must be removed from arbitrary positions but the heap only supports removing the top, mark them as deleted in a side structure and discard stale entries as they surface.
important_details: Keep a HashMap of pending deletions keyed by value (with counts), and a counter of how many stale entries each heap currently holds.
Before any peek or poll, drain the top while it matches a pending deletion — this keeps each deletion O(log n) amortized instead of O(n).
Necessary because Java's PriorityQueue.remove(Object) is O(n), which turns a sliding-window solution into O(n*k).
Track logical sizes separately from heap.size(), since the heaps contain stale entries that should not count.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(log n) amortized per operation. Space: O(n) including stale entries.

variations.description: Repeatedly extract the two cheapest items, combine them, and push the result back — the greedy pattern behind Huffman coding, rope/stone merging, and minimum-cost connection problems.
important_details: The exchange-argument proof: combining the two smallest items first minimizes the number of times any single item is re-counted in the total cost.
Each combination reduces the item count by one, so the loop runs exactly n-1 times for n items.
Watch for integer overflow when costs accumulate — use long for the running total on large inputs.
Do NOT apply this greedy blindly to interval-DP problems like 'burst balloons' or matrix chain multiplication, where merging order is constrained and DP is required.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n log n). Space: O(n).
